sentences.text: The name Cryodrakon translates to 'cold dragon' in Greek, referencing the icy climate of its discovery site, while the species name boreas honors the Greek god of the north winds.
Cryodrakon is estimated to have had a wingspan of about 10 meters, making it one of the largest flying animals in history.
A large incomplete neck vertebra measuring 40 cm suggests that adult Cryodrakon could have had a vertebra at least 50 cm long.
Michael Habib considered 'viserion' as a species name, referencing the ice dragon from Game of Thrones.
Paleontologists David Hone, Michael Habib, and François Therrien formally named and described this species in 2019.
The holotype specimen, catalogued as TMP 1992.83, was uncovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta in 1992.
Large azhdarchid bones had been reported from Alberta since 1972, but early finds were often assigned to the genus Quetzalcoatlus due to limited knowledge of North American relatives at the time.
Diet: Cryodrakon likely hunted smaller animals on the ground, a behavior similar to that of modern marabou storks.
Health: The holotype skeleton showed evidence of being scavenged by a dromaeosaurid, possibly Saurornitholestes langstoni.
Health: A broken tooth found embedded in a Cryodrakon bone suggests its thin-walled bones were very tough.
Health: A 2025 study found probable bite marks on a juvenile Cryodrakon vertebra from various possible predators or scavengers.
Cryodrakon is classified within the pterosaur family Azhdarchidae, which includes the famous genus Quetzalcoatlus.
Later studies placed Cryodrakon within the subfamily Quetzalcoatlinae, though its exact position varies between analyses.
Researchers noted features that exclude Cryodrakon from a basal position within Azhdarchidae, though a full phylogenetic analysis was not performed due to fragmentary remains.
The only known species of Cryodrakon is Cryodrakon boreas.
Cryodrakon boreas lived in what is now Canada during the late Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 76.7 to 74.3 million years ago.
This time period falls within the broader Campanian stage, which spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
Fossils come from the Dinosaur Park Formation, which preserves alluvial and coastal plain environments.
